title: Grimms’ Fairy Tales
author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm
estimatedTime: About 7 hours in all; each tale takes minutes
openingText: A certain king had a beautiful garden, and in the garden grew a tree that bore golden apples. The apples were counted regularly, and just as they were starting to ripen, the king found that one went missing every night.
about:
Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm gathered these tales from oral sources and published them in German in 1812 and 1814. This English text is based on the translations of Edgar Taylor and Marian Edwardes and presents 65 tales as separate reading units, from the golden apples of the opening story to Snow-White and Rose-Red at the close.

The stories are short, direct and repeated in patterns. A king loses golden apples, a poor man trades a lump of gold for a horse, a fisherman’s wife keeps asking for more. Things come in threes, rhymes recur word for word, and helpers appear to those who treat them well. Some tales are comic, some are cruel, and a few end without a clear moral. The narrator rarely explains.

You can read the tales in any order or straight through. Familiar titles such as Hansel and Gretel, Rapunzel, Little Red-Cap and Briar Rose sit beside less familiar ones, including Cat and Mouse in Partnership and The Juniper-Tree. In this collection the story known as Snow White appears under the title Snowdrop.

whyItMatters.title: The tales state cruelty and reward plainly
whyItMatters.body: Hansel and Gretel are left in a forest by their own parents, and the witch who lives in the house they begin to eat prepares an oven for Gretel. The narrator reports these events at the same pace as a meal or a journey. Punishment and reward follow from what each character has done, and the collection leaves readers to judge them. A reader today may notice how much the tales trust listeners with difficult material.

whyItMatters.title: Repetition and rhyme carry the stories
whyItMatters.body: The fisherman returns to the sea to speak the same rhyme each time his wife wants more, and only the size of her demand changes: a cottage, a castle, a throne, finally the sun and moon. Rumpelstiltskin, the Goose-Girl and the Juniper-Tree each depend on a fixed verse that returns exactly. These repeated lines give the tales their rhythm and their suspense. The same device appears now in children’s picture books and in the chants of online games.

whyItMatters.title: Many familiar plots appear in plainer, stranger forms
whyItMatters.body: Little Red-Cap, for instance, includes a second encounter with a wolf that many retellings leave out. The collection also holds stories of tailors, soldiers, peasants and animals that never became famous. Reading them together shows how many kinds of story one collection can hold. Going back to the source of a familiar film plot is a quick way to see what changed.

angleCards.title: Follow the repeated lines
angleCards.text: Notice which verses and formulas return unchanged, and what changes around them each time.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Grimms’ Fairy Tales to follow how repeated rhymes and formulas build suspense and shape each story.

angleCards.title: Compare the helpers and the tests
angleCards.text: Track who helps the hero, what they are asked in return, and which small kindnesses or refusals decide the ending.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Grimms’ Fairy Tales to examine how characters earn help or lose it through small choices.

angleCards.title: Meet the lesser-known tales
angleCards.text: Read beyond Hansel and Gretel and Rapunzel to the tailors, the animals and the foolish and clever peasants.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Grimms’ Fairy Tales to discover the lesser-known stories and see how they differ from the famous ones.

angleCards.title: Read the cruelty closely
angleCards.text: Notice how punishments are described and how the narrator frames them, and ask what each tale seems to want from its audience.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Grimms’ Fairy Tales to understand how the stories present violence, justice and consequence.
